brief.head: Tyranny of the larks
brief.text: Amit Varma, a night owl, accused Ajay Shah, a morning lark, of complicity in “the tyranny of the larks”. About thirty per cent of people are night owls, he said. {100-R01}

brief.text: A Federal Reserve official or someone at a financial firm speaks within institutional limits, Ajay Shah said. Behind constrained writing there is often “a full bubbling mind”. {100-C05}

lead.kicker: Episode 100: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah take questions
lead.head: A century, and still not out
body: A hundred episodes ago, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah made what Shah called “a pact signed in blood”: they would find the bloody-mindedness to reach Episode 100, and then ask whether the show was worth doing. {#pact}

Shah’s verdict was yes, though a weekly show had been hard and he worried about “creeping to the edges of expertise”. He apologised, gentle reader, if he had on occasion misrepresented his standard errors.
Varma’s idea of the show had always been looser: bring frames from one field to bear on another, and talk without pretending to certainty, as long as you are transparent that you are speculating.
For the century they took readers’ questions, tersely rephrased by Shah, and answered them for an hour and a half, from broken academic incentives to shampoo.
## Thoughtful people

The first question set the tone: what separates thoughtful people from the rest? Self-reflection, Varma said. Once you internalise it, it becomes a virtuous cycle, and you seek out others who reflect too.
Most people never do it, he said, especially men. A friend of his, a CXO at a big company, finds his fellow executives have nothing to talk about but cricket, Bollywood and office gossip.
Varma learnt his own economics and biology without a degree in either. Find a field’s first principles, he said, such as scarcity, incentives or natural selection, and the rest of the field opens up.
“If it’s a rabbit hole, just get into the rabbit hole and the more you read and at some point the fog clears and you see the bigger picture,” he said. {100-C09}
Shah, who read biology for pleasure as a PhD student, finds that his work increasingly comes from other people: arguing with them, and being corrected by them.
## Do the work
On creating things, Varma was frank: 99 per cent of the things he had wanted to do, he had not done. {#undone} What he does have, he said, is a bias for action.
Asked how to build an audience on Substack, he called the question a trap. Beginners are bad, they get no audience, and if validation matters they quit before they get good. {100-C12}
Reading, he argued, is how we collect the dots we join to picture the world. “The more dots there are, the more high definition our picture will be.”
## India, and the end

On India, Shah was the optimist. For the first time in a century, he said, the country is building a critical mass of intellectual capacity, helped by the internet. “A country cannot be better than its elite,” he said.
Varma had less faith in the elite. India’s default religion, he said, is the religion of the state, and most young people still expect it to solve every problem.
Asked what part of Indian life is fatally misaligned with modernity, he named conventional marriage. For most of India, he said, “marriage is death for women”.
Asked how he keeps his humour, Varma pointed to mortality. Next to the certainty of death, every other tragedy shrinks, and stressing over an article becomes laughable. {100-C22}
Shah’s version was to live fully and delight in being alive. “Everything is everything,” he said, “and everything will die.”
And the show? It will go on, Varma said, “not because we like the show”, but because they like the company.

second.label: Artificial intelligence
second.head: Mind the luggage rack
second.deck: Amit Varma toured Spain’s museums with ChatGPT, and found where to put his bag
body: Travelling through Spain, Amit Varma had ChatGPT’s Deep Research write reports of some twenty thousand words before each museum: the Picasso Museum, the Prado, the Reina Sofia. Each set out the artists’ phases, the key works room by room, and the order to walk through them. {100-S08}
Before a train from Barcelona to Madrid, he asked where to put a huge bag. The AI asked which train, then named the coach and showed, with a photograph, the luggage racks at either end.
Judging AI by its current state, he said, is like judging computing by a mainframe that filled a room in 1954. {100-C29} He still checks the sources. “A lot of it is how deeply you prompt.”

quote.text: So it’s a complete Google replacement for me.

second.caption: touring Spain with ChatGPT

third.head: Late bloomers
body: Amit Varma has recently seen several real cases of the same thing: an old woman whose husband has died suddenly becomes a new person. “It’s like she’s free, she’s blooming, she’s learning an instrument, or she’s travelling solo,” he said. {100-S09}
Such women may never have felt confined, he said: marriage was the structure they flowed into, it was normalised, and no alternative ever seemed to exist.

Varma tied this to Chinmay Tumbe’s *India Moving*: the largest internal migration in India happens when women marry and move to the husband’s village. They lose their childhood friends, and often even their names.

For most of India, Varma said, marriage destroys women’s agency and individuality. {100-C19} He granted that tradition has its reassurances, and that finding love on dating apps is deeply complicated too.
third.caption: the widows who bloom

p2.title: Ask me everything
p2.deck: Four themes ran through the hundredth episode’s answers: learning, making, India and living

sections.label: On learning
sections.head: Read a lot, forget a lot
sections.caption: reading, remembering and writing
body: What separates thoughtful people from the rest? Amit Varma found it a little pompous to divide the world that way, but answered: self-reflection, which most people, especially men, never do. {100-C02}
Six readers asked the same question: how do you remember all this? Varma forgets the details within a week, keeps copious notes in Roam Research, and lets volume do the rest. {100-C10}
The risk is repetition. He curses himself for not reading enough, he said, each time he repeats Bob Dylan’s “he not busy being born is busy dying”.
## Adjacencies

Ajay Shah added adjacencies. Topology bewilders a newcomer but comes easily after calculus and real analysis, because we remember what connects richly to what we already know. Each use of a memory, he said, refreshes it, like a static RAM cell.

On writing, Varma uses the frame of stock and flow. Flow is blogs and columns, a writing gym: he wrote some eight thousand blog posts from 2003 to 2008, none, he thinks, worth preserving. {#posts} Stock is books, and he has not made enough.
Shah writes his columns and LEAP blog posts with a researcher’s push for novelty, so they become stock he can reuse. “So I feel books are the leap of integration,” he said. {100-C14}

~ Shah drew a sobering lesson from academia, where publication bias rewards sensation and million-fold rises in research spending have disappointed: “When you put up really high powered incentives, the people will goddamn pursue them.”

quote.text: So if you just read a lot, the memorable stuff will stick with you, whether you take a note or not.

sections.label: On making
sections.head: Write first, audience later
sections.caption: doing the work
body: Amit Varma’s confession was that he gets weekly shows done on deadline and looks efficient, while the books he deeply wants to write wait. The book he wrote in 2008 does not make him terribly happy. {#book}
Asked how to build a Substack audience, he refused the premise. “A good product is the best marketing,” he said. Write first; the audience comes later, organically. {100-C12}
The hosts committed to 104 episodes, two years, before taking a call on the show, knowing they would be bad at first. {#pact104} Varma, who has “a face for audio”, keeps putting episodes out anyway.
## The thirty per cent

Nomsita, who sits behind the camera, asked how creative people can nurture their souls and still earn a living. Varma, once a copywriter, an MTV scriptwriter and a journalist, said that if 70 per cent of your work is drudgery and 30 per cent satisfies you, you are lucky. {100-C26}

Be bloody-minded about protecting the thirty per cent, he said, and bring care to the drudgery, since that is where you learn the craft. As success comes, do not let the ratio drift to a hundred and nothing.
~ He has pushed friends the same way. Mohit Satyanand started a newsletter after one of Varma’s lectures on bias for action, and in about three years has not missed a Sunday. {100-S05}

quote.text: You’re very lucky to have that thirty per cent.

sections.label: On India
sections.head: The state as a religion
sections.caption: India’s future
body: Ajay Shah is “very bullish” on politicians. Vijay Kelkar taught him that officials are trained into conservatism while politicians are entrepreneurs, walking thousands of kilometres and knowing far more about farm distress and jobs than their slogans let on. {100-C03}
Amit Varma pushed back: if politics is downstream of culture, populist demand will get populist supply. Great leadership, Shah replied, is doing more than following the polls.
Shah is optimistic that the statism of the bad years from 1914 to 1945 is fading as India globalises and grows comfortable with markets. {#statism}

Varma, who meets more young people, disagreed. Most, he said, still look to the state as parent and provider and want it to fix every problem. Because zero-sum, top-down thinking is hardwired, each generation must fight the battle anew. {100-C20}
## Maps keep changing

Asked about nation-states, Varma noted that India has been one for only about 78 years. {#nation} Maps change all the time, he said, and the internet let both hosts swap communities of circumstance for communities of choice.
Shah named two high-probability troubles ahead: a dramatic fall in fertility that will bring rapid ageing, and global warming that is already baked in. {#fertility}
~ Varma would not call anything inevitable. The world of 2040 cannot be pictured today, and that, for him, is a reason for hope.

quote.text: I find that the fact that it is unknown unknowns is actually a cause of hope

sections.label: On living
sections.head: Play the hand you’re dealt
sections.caption: money, luck and mortality
body: Asked how to think about money, Ajay Shah offered one line: it is like blood. You need it to live, but it is not the way to keep score in the video game. {100-C15}
Amit Varma added that money feels like the binding constraint when you are young. Over a whole life, he said, the real scarcity is time: “That’s what you will definitely run out of.”

Five years of professional poker taught Varma to think in probabilities, which made him less certain, less judgemental and less proud of his successes. “I know that ninety nine per cent of everything is luck,” he said. {100-C07}
## No victims

A reader asked what to do without the nurturing that shaped Shah. Everyone is dealt a random hand of cards, he replied, and the only interesting question is what you do next, not whining about structural injustice. {100-C23}
The worst thing a person can do, Varma said, is wrap themselves in a narrative of victimhood: your circumstances of birth do not define you.
~ On hard times, Varma advised cherishing small happinesses and soldiering through. Nobody, he said, is a perfectly rational man immune to the stormy forces of life.

quote.text: Money is like blood. You need money to live, but it’s not the point of living.

side.boxText: The hosts held an earlier Ask Me Anything at Episode 50, the halfway mark. Readers sent questions through a form, and Ajay Shah, who sorted them, rephrased each one tersely. Amit Varma marked the moment as one of “great celebration, perhaps even great relief”. {100-R29}

contQuote.text: And the internet freed both of us, and certainly for me it’s a very big deal that I could form communities of choice. And geography was no longer destiny

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: How the hosts learnt, quit, made pacts and lived through history

stories.start: I think the answer is curiosity. Namisha is right, I did a BA
stories.end: at some point the fog clears and you see the bigger picture
stories.caption: his six classes
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on his education, formal and otherwise
stories.head: The six-lecture degree
body: Amit Varma’s degree is a BA in English literature from Fergusson College in Pune. He attended, he reckons, about six classes in the three years combined. {100-S02}
Why literature? “I only chose English literature because I knew I wouldn’t have to study,” he said. He coasted through those years, endlessly curious and reading a lot.

His real education came one first principle at a time. Steven Pinker’s *The Blank Slate* was his gateway to natural selection, after which he read all of Richard Dawkins, *The Selfish Gene*, *The Blind Watchmaker*, “the whole shebang”, and then Daniel Dennett and Robert Wright. {100-R03}
He quoted Douglas Adams, who said that once he understood natural selection there was no need to believe in God, preferring the awe of knowledge to the awe of ignorance.

Economics went the same way: Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson*, Frédéric Bastiat, and popular books such as Tim Harford’s *The Logic of Life*. You need not run regressions, he said; you need scarcity and incentives to become part of how you think. {100-R05}
He has used economic thinking to break down cricket strategy. Then there were five years of professional poker, which taught him to think in a Bayesian way.
~ It was always fun, he said, never work: find a new subject, dive in, and do not ask what productive thing will come out of it. That, he thinks, is how most people are.
stories.why: Credentials are not the gate. Once a field’s first principles click, whether scarcity and incentives or natural selection, the rest of the field opens up, and its tools can be carried elsewhere, as Varma carried economics into cricket. {100-C09}

stories.caption: a pact made on a boat in Kochi
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a writers’ pact made in Kochi
stories.head: The boat stayed, one book sailed
body: Two years ago, at a conference in Kochi, Amit Varma, Lancelot Pinto and Vasant Dhar were taken to a boat for a ride. A storm started, and the boat never went anywhere. {100-S06}
So they stood on the boat, looking out at the water, talking about the books each of them wanted to write. They made a pact: by the next year’s conference, all three would have written one.
Varma had earlier pushed Dhar to start a newsletter in a personal tone, then to write a book in that voice. Two years on, Dhar has just sent his final manuscript to his publisher. {#manuscript}
~ Varma and Pinto have not. Whenever they meet, they marvel at Vasant, and hope to be inspired by him.

quote.text: by the time this conference comes about next year, all three of us would have written a book

stories.postscript: Ajay Shah and Akshay Jaitly, both surrounded by friends who write books, each plan a shelf of signed copies only. {100-S07}

stories.start: Yeah, so I was always curious about the world.
stories.end: I know how I was surprised when the wicks crossed 68 and so on
stories.caption: a life of global dramas
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on living through history as it happened
stories.head: Front-row seat to every crisis
body: Ajay Shah never accepted the narrow track where you specialise and orient yourself to publication. As a PhD student, he was endlessly reading biology on the side.

Looking back, he sees one deep dive into a global drama after another: the Asian crisis, 9/11 and Islamic extremism, the Afghanistan wars, the 2008 financial crisis, the pandemic and modern populism. “So I’m the child of all these big global dramatic events that happened,” he said. {100-S04}
Amit Varma recalled the old Chinese curse, may you live in interesting times. For Shah it seemed a blessing, Varma said, “which can only mean you’re a sociopath”. {100-J05}

~ Shah said he was thrilled to have lived through it. Reading about the Great Depression is different, he said, from being there: watching the data, knowing who said what on which date, being surprised when the VIX crossed 68. {#vix}
stories.why: A broad base in science, statistics, economics and history gives you entry gates into each new crisis, Shah said. With them, every unfolding event becomes a live seminar rather than a headline.

stories.start: The other um situation I am in which is both good fortune
stories.end: I don't have to go down particular tracks. And that has sort of helped.
stories.caption: quitting the company life
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the job he decided never to have
stories.head: Notice served, for good
body: Around 2006 or 2007, Amit Varma was managing editor of Cricinfo. Some seventeen years ago, he said, he decided he would never do a job again. {100-S03}

He moved to a consulting role as contributing editor for a couple of years, then left entirely. He wrote a book, played professional poker for five years and edited *Pragati*, a policy magazine, for the Takshashila Institution, remotely and part-time.
The choice, he said, did not always seem like good fortune. But it gave him time to read what he wants, when he wants, without being pushed down particular tracks.
~ He has not been as intentional about the knowledge life as he would like, he admitted, and Ajay Shah has done better. When a guest has written eight books, Varma reads all eight. {#eightbooks}

quote.text: I was never a company man, and that gives me the time to read when I want, read what I want.

quiz.a: English literature, because he knew he would not have to study.

quiz.q: In a single line on money, what did Ajay Shah compare it to?
quiz.a: Blood: you need money to live, but it is not the point of living.

quiz.q: Which book did Varma cite for the claim that roughly thirty per cent of people are night owls?
quiz.a: *Why We Sleep* by Matthew Walker, which Varma called an excellent book.

quiz.q: According to Chinmay Tumbe’s book, as cited by Amit Varma, what causes India’s largest internal migration?
quiz.a: Marriage: women move from their own village to their husband’s village.

quiz.q: From whom did Ajay Shah learn that only politicians, not officials, are entrepreneurs?
quiz.a: Vijay Kelkar, who taught him that officials are ingrained around conservatism.

quiz.a: Which coach to board, and where the luggage racks were, with a photograph.
